topic-040-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.evolution: Early representatives study dependent, mortal, and infinitely many arms. Later work develops subset selection and adaptive identification. Recent methods track optimal allocations in linear models and pairwise ranking, while new analyses compare fixed-budget and fixed-confidence settings and extend experimental design to assortment selection.
openQuestions: How can optimal allocations be tracked cheaply when the candidate set is enormous?
What stopping rules remain reliable under model misspecification or changing alternatives?
topic-040-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.overview: Pure exploration uses sequential measurements to identify the best option or subset, rather than maximize reward while learning. This cluster covers linear and combinatorial bandits, dependent or changing arms, and noisy pairwise comparisons. Algorithms allocate observations adaptively and stop when the evidence supports a decision at a specified confidence level.
topic-040-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.title: Best-Arm Identification and Pure Exploration
topic-040-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.whyItMatters: Uniform sampling can waste effort on clearly inferior options while neglecting close competitors. Instance-sensitive lower bounds reveal where information is needed and help separate statistical efficiency from the cost of computing a sampling plan.

topic-041-understanding-instance-level-i.evolution: Early representatives address aggregation bias, equal opportunity, and causal discrimination. Later work studies demographic-free reweighting and instance-level interventions. Recent examples estimate dataset-specific fairness frontiers with uncertainty and organize path-specific counterfactual notions into a hierarchy, broadening how fairness claims can be interpreted and compared.
openQuestions: How should uncertainty in a learned causal graph affect fairness conclusions?
Which tradeoffs remain acceptable after deployment changes the population or its behavior?
topic-041-understanding-instance-level-i.overview: Fairness methods examine how predictions differ across groups, which training examples drive those differences, and which uses of sensitive information are acceptable. This cluster includes statistical constraints, reweighting, influence analysis, counterfactual modeling, and fairness–utility tradeoffs. Different definitions encode different choices about the harms a model should avoid.
topic-041-understanding-instance-level-i.title: Fair Prediction and Causal Fairness
topic-041-understanding-instance-level-i.whyItMatters: A fairness requirement cannot be evaluated independently of the dataset, uncertainty, and intended decision. Quantifying achievable tradeoffs and causal pathways can make disagreements explicit instead of hiding them behind a single disparity score.

topic-042-a-bayesian-approach-for-policy.evolution: Earlier representatives combine heuristic search, game-tree evaluation, and temporal-difference learning. Later methods add Bayesian and maximum-entropy planning. The 2024–2026 evidence develops parallel particle-based policy optimization and analyzes why branching into multiple continuations can reduce an uncertainty floor that additional independent thoughts alone cannot remove.
openQuestions: How should a planner allocate samples between breadth and repeated evaluation of promising branches?
When do model errors invalidate apparent gains from deeper search?
topic-042-a-bayesian-approach-for-policy.overview: Sampling-based planners evaluate possible futures without enumerating every action sequence. This topic includes Monte Carlo tree search, sequential Monte Carlo, Bayesian adaptation, and policy improvement through search. Recent work also studies branching over reasoning continuations, where the allocation of samples affects the accuracy of learning signals.
topic-042-a-bayesian-approach-for-policy.title: Monte Carlo Planning and Search-Based Policy Improvement
topic-042-a-bayesian-approach-for-policy.whyItMatters: Search quality depends on where computation is spent, not only how many rollouts are generated. Parallel sampling and variance-aware allocation can make planning more scalable while preserving useful distinctions among candidate actions or thoughts.

topic-043-exploration-a-study-of-count-b.evolution: The collection spans active exploration from the early 1990s to optimistic model selection and modern reward-agnostic navigation. Recent work incorporates retrospective transition structure and constraint-aware intrinsic rewards. Newer examples address environmental drift and combine low-rank reward completion with uncertainty-based fallback to exploration when structural assumptions are unreliable.
openQuestions: Which intrinsic objectives discover reusable knowledge rather than task-irrelevant novelty?
How can an agent recognize when a structural reward model should be abandoned?
topic-043-exploration-a-study-of-count-b.overview: An agent must discover useful behavior even when external rewards are rare or delayed. These papers develop intrinsic rewards, reward-free exploration, optimism, and information-seeking policies. Some methods use both past and possible future transitions to recognize bottlenecks, while others exploit structure in the reward function itself.
topic-043-exploration-a-study-of-count-b.title: Exploration with Sparse Rewards and Changing Environments
topic-043-exploration-a-study-of-count-b.whyItMatters: Visiting many states is not necessarily informative exploration. Effective strategies should reveal controllable routes, resolve uncertainty relevant to future tasks, and avoid confusing randomness or repeated failure with useful novelty.

topic-044-a-collective-learning-framewor.evolution: Earlier representatives develop network metrics and inductive graph representations. Later work scales contrastive learning and handles federated or non-IID graphs. Recent methods reshape connectivity to improve label influence and combine textual semantics with topology to reject, annotate, and incorporate previously unknown classes.
openQuestions: How can learned graph edits be validated when labels are scarce?
What prevents automatic unknown-class annotation from reinforcing its own mistakes?
topic-044-a-collective-learning-framewor.overview: Graph learners combine node features, connections, and scarce labels to predict or classify relational data. This cluster studies contrastive objectives, learned graph structure, semi-supervision, and distribution differences across graphs. Recent open-world methods also confront unlabeled nodes that belong to classes absent from training.
topic-044-a-collective-learning-framewor.title: Graph Learning with Limited Labels and Unknown Classes
topic-044-a-collective-learning-framewor.whyItMatters: Message passing can spread useful supervision, but it can also propagate misleading relationships or assume every node belongs to a known category. A reliable learner must decide both what information to share and when the current label vocabulary is incomplete.

topic-045-a-computer-simulation-of-olfac.evolution: The earliest representatives model olfactory and sparse distributed memory. Later work studies correlations, kernel memories, and biological key-value learning. Recent examples introduce fixed scaffolds for graceful recall, long-sequence Hopfield models, temporal-context reinstatement, and theoretical phase changes in forgetting under low-rank adaptation.
openQuestions: How can memory capacity be measured when partial recall remains useful?
Which interventions preserve old associations without blocking the acquisition of new ones?
topic-045-a-computer-simulation-of-olfac.overview: Associative memory retrieves stored content from partial cues, but capacity and interference determine whether old information survives new learning. This topic includes attractor networks, key-value memories, sequence storage, and biologically inspired scaffolds. Related analyses study how changes to modern neural representations can trigger catastrophic forgetting.
topic-045-a-computer-simulation-of-olfac.title: Associative Memory, Sequence Recall, and Forgetting
topic-045-a-computer-simulation-of-olfac.whyItMatters: A memory system should degrade gracefully when its capacity is exceeded rather than abruptly lose everything. Separating stable internal organization from the content attached to it offers one route to balancing storage, recall fidelity, and continued learning.

topic-046-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.evolution: Early representatives analyze nonsmooth learning and online gradient dynamics. Later work proves convergence under overparameterization and studies simplicity bias in shallow networks. Recent papers characterize local minima, linear-region structure, depth-dependent bias, and width-independent sensitivity bounds in specified initialization or lazy-training regimes.
openQuestions: Which conclusions extend beyond highly overparameterized or lazy-training settings?
How do optimization-friendly landscapes interact with robustness and the complexity of the learned function?
topic-046-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.overview: Neural optimization is nonconvex, yet wide networks often fit their training data efficiently. This topic studies how width, depth, initialization, nonsmooth activations, and gradient dynamics shape that behavior. It also asks which solutions training prefers and how properties such as margins or local sensitivity relate to learned representations.
topic-046-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.title: Neural Loss Geometry and Implicit Learning Bias
topic-046-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.whyItMatters: Successful interpolation does not by itself explain generalization or robustness. The geometry that permits optimization and the bias that selects among solutions are distinct pieces of a useful theory.

topic-047-a-bayesian-analysis-of-algorit.evolution: The collection reaches back to rule and pattern learning in 1983. Later titles emphasize statistical rule induction and empirical classifier comparison. The available recent abstracts focus on unifying definitions of disentanglement and separating data limitations from compatibility between a learning algorithm and a composition rule; they do not establish a direct historical dependency.
openQuestions: Which definitions of disentanglement are appropriate for stochastic rather than deterministic representations?
How can experiments isolate knowledge composition from ordinary distributional coverage?
topic-047-a-bayesian-analysis-of-algorit.overview: This broad foundations cluster examines what a learner represents as a concept and how learned knowledge transfers to new combinations. Historical examples concern rules, hypothesis filtering, noisy data, and comparisons of supervised methods. Recent representatives formalize disentanglement, diversity, and the statistical conditions needed to compose knowledge across distributions.
topic-047-a-bayesian-analysis-of-algorit.title: Concept Learning and Compositional Generalization
topic-047-a-bayesian-analysis-of-algorit.whyItMatters: Terms such as concept, factor, or composition can refer to different mathematical objects. Clear definitions help distinguish a genuine transfer ability from success caused by more data, easier examples, or a favorable evaluation protocol.
